sources.news_title: Trump reverses Pentagon plan to livestream Nidal Hasan's scheduled execution
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said Thursday that the scheduled Dec. 3 firing-squad execution of former Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan will not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon plan.
Trump wrote on Truth Social that streaming the execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” but that “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.”
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump said. He added that immediate family members of the victims may view the execution in person “if they so choose” and that “They deserve to witness JUSTICE!”
Hasan was convicted in 2013 of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a Nov. 5, 2009, shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. He opened fire inside the Soldier Readiness Processing Center while soldiers prepared for deployment, shouting “Allahu Akbar.” Among those killed was Pvt. Francheska Velez, who was pregnant; her unborn child also died.
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle set the execution for 1 p.m. Central time on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of the attack. The Pentagon announced earlier this month that Trump had approved War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s recommendation for death by Army firing squad. It would be the U.S. military’s first execution since 1961 and the first by firing squad since World War II.
Trump’s post also referenced the FBI’s handling of communications between Hasan and radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki before the attack. Under the Obama administration, investigators reviewed intercepted electronic messages and concluded they did not constitute a threat. A later independent review led by former FBI Director William Webster identified shortcomings in information sharing, database use, and coordination between field offices as a significant intelligence failure. The Army was not notified of the contacts before the shooting.
The plan to livestream the execution, which Hegseth had described as public, drew criticism. Vice President JD Vance said he would not watch it.
Hasan, who is paralyzed from the waist down from wounds sustained when he was shot by responding officers, has exhausted his military appeals. The Supreme Court declined to review his case in March of 2025.

Trump cancels planned livestream of Fort Hood attacker’s execution
US President Donald Trump has withdrawn plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army psychiatrist responsible for the deadly 2009 shooting at Fort Hood in Texas.
Trump had earlier supported broadcasting Hasan’s execution by firing squad, arguing that showing the punishment could discourage terrorism. However, he changed his position following widespread criticism from human rights organisations and members of the public in the United States and other countries.
Announcing the decision on Thursday, Trump said some people opposed to the broadcast had good intentions.
“Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die,” he said.
The president explained that he had initially viewed the livestream as a possible warning to others who might engage in terrorism.
“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He added that the decision to cancel the broadcast would not affect the planned execution.
“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” the president said.
Hasan killed 13 unarmed US military personnel and wounded 32 others during the shooting at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in November 2009.
The US military announced that his execution would take place on December 3, 2026, making it the first military execution in the United States in more than 60 years.
Although the execution will no longer be broadcast publicly, Trump said relatives of the victims would still be allowed to attend and witness it in person if they wished.
The Pentagon’s earlier announcement that the execution would be livestreamed sparked strong reactions, with human rights advocates and other critics questioning the decision to turn a death sentence into a public spectacle.
The United Nations also condemned the proposal, describing the planned broadcast as abhorrent.
Figures from Amnesty International show that thousands of executions were recorded worldwide in 2025. However, public executions were reported in only two countries.
The organisation documented 11 public executions in Iran and six in Afghanistan during the year, highlighting how uncommon the practice remains internationally.

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump rejected plans to livestream the execution of a former Army major who killed 13 people in 2009, overruling Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s proposal after facing intense bipartisan backlash.
Trump said Thursday the execution would proceed, and that it may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, “but this event will not be livestreamed.”
“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” the president posted on social media.
Hegseth announced last week that Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad would be broadcast publicly. The U.S. stopped public executions decades ago and critics argued that livestreaming the killing of Hasan, who is confined to a wheelchair, would look barbaric and amount to a propaganda win for extremist groups.
Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood in Killeen, Texas, in Nov. 2009, killing 13 and wounding more than 30 before he was shot in the back and subdued. He’s set to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3. Hasan has said he wants to die a martyr, and Hegseth’s critics argued that a livestream would fulfill that wish.
Vice President JD Vance was the most prominent administration figure to express doubt about the plan and said he wouldn’t watch. The conservative-leaning opinion page of the Wall Street Journal also published an op-ed opposing the livestream.
“It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, wrote on X. “How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself.”
The idea put renewed scrutiny on Hegseth, who has used his position as defense secretary to emphasize what he says is a more lethal fighting force and to champion Trump’s opposition to diversity, equity and inclusion practices. His livestream announcement prompted Democrats to renew calls for his removal. Many have voiced plans to try to impeach him if they gain control of the House of Representatives in November’s midterm election.
Trump’s decision not to broadcast the livestream also allows the military to avoid a host of legal challenges. Most social-media platforms prohibit disseminating videos and images that show death or glorify violence.

Putting out a dancing Nidal Hasan over his kill count.’ I don't think some 35-year-old dude is doing that,” he said. “You have a younger generation that is now attuned to what he did.”
Livestreaming the public execution would have given propagandists more to work with. Online nihilists, gore groups, and Islamists often use footage of death and violence to lure in young people. “Dead ideologues are continually being revered, lionized in ecosystems in support of groups like Al Qaeda, the Islamic State, or any terrorist group,” Ayad said. “If you look at the saint ecosystems around accelerationism, it's a similar thing in which these individuals are the vanguard of jihad.”
Mass shooters and ideological killers that receive widespread media attention become objects of fascination online. They enter a cannon of sainted killers, totems that inspire others to commit the same acts. Some researchers have suggested news agencies should report a shooter’s crimes but refrain from naming and showing them, thus depriving them of notoriety and stemming the social contagion.
Hasan killed people almost twenty years ago and he was destined to fall out of memory until Hegseth attempted to make a spectacle of his death. “We’re already seeing it being incorporated into talking points, we’re past that,” Ayad said.
“He is still going to be labeled a martyr," Ayad added. “Will it be a public spectacle? Not anymore [...] but terror groups and their supporters took advantage of the news to highlight just how much of a contribution Nidal Hasan made to their respective movements.”

sources.news_title: Trump cancels Pentagon plans to livestream firing squad execution
sources.text:
On Thursday, Donald Trump called off the Pentagon’s highly controversial plans to livestream a firing squad execution that is still on schedule for December 3.
Trump supports the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood. But sources close to Trump told CNN that the president was blindsided last week when Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the event—which is the first US execution of a soldier since World War II—would be livestreamed.
Backlash to the livestream was immediate and crossed political divides. On the morning Trump canceled the plans, an ABC News poll found 8 in 10 Americans were against the livestream, including a 55 percent majority of MAGA Republicans.
Insiders told ABC News that Trump feared that “broadcasting the execution could super charge anti-American propaganda or reflect poorly on the US.” Privately, Trump had remarked that “he did not initially know that Hasan was paralyzed from the waist down,” CNN reported. As one Army officer appalled by Hegseth’s announcement explained in a separate CNN report, livestreaming the execution “takes away everything America stands for.”
“The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable,” the officer, who was deployed multiple times in the Middle East, told CNN.
Livestream risked identifying US soldiers
On Truth Social, Trump confirmed that Hasan “will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.” Families of victims will still be able to watch the execution, but the execution will not be broadcast for the public.

Trump Cancels Fort Hood Shooter's Execution Livestream, Says People 'Would Rather Not Watch Him Die'
Hasan's execution by firing squad remains scheduled for 3 December 2026
US President Donald Trump has scrapped plans to livestream Nidal Malik Hasan's scheduled execution, saying many people would rather not watch him die.
Trump announced the decision on Thursday, 15 October, following bipartisan criticism of the proposed broadcast. Hasan's execution by firing squad remains scheduled for 3 December 2026.
Trump Scraps Hasan Execution Livestream
In a social media post, Trump acknowledged that broadcasting the execution might have served as a deterrent but said many people would prefer not to witness it.
He said publicly airing the execution 'might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan'.
However, he added that 'many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device'.
'He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,' Trump wrote.
Trump said the victims' immediate families could witness the execution in person if they wished.
Vice President JD Vance had also expressed reservations about watching the execution and questioned whether the proposed livestream would take place.
Asked earlier this month how a public execution would align with his Christian faith, Vance said: 'I don't know that that's actually going to happen.'
Vance stressed the seriousness of Hasan's crimes, saying the controversy over the execution should not overshadow the victims. 'I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,' he said.
The vice president added: 'Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it.'
His remarks stopped short of calling for the broadcast to be cancelled.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had announced earlier this month that Hasan's execution would be public. The Pentagon subsequently confirmed the livestream plan, prompting criticism that broadcasting an execution could provide propaganda material for extremists.
Fort Hood Shooting Killed 13 People
Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist, carried out the attack at Fort Hood, a US military installation in Texas, on 5 November 2009. He opened fire in a medical building where soldiers were preparing for deployment. The attack killed 13 people and wounded dozens of others.
The shooting led to a military prosecution, and Hasan was convicted and sentenced to death in 2013.
Hasan said he wanted to prevent soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan and killing fellow Muslims. However, a military judge barred him from presenting that argument as a defence during his 2013 trial.
Trump approved his execution by firing squad earlier this month. The planned broadcast then became a separate point of controversy, drawing criticism from both Republicans and Democrats.
The debate concerned whether the execution should be shown publicly, rather than whether Hasan had been convicted of the killings.
Execution Date Remains Unchanged
The Pentagon has said Hasan's execution is scheduled for 3 December 2026. Trump's announcement withdraws the public broadcast without cancelling the execution itself.
Trump had presented a livestream as a possible deterrent, while critics warned that distributing footage could amplify extremist messaging. Those competing arguments formed part of the debate over the proposed broadcast, rather than established conclusions about its likely effects.
The reversal follows bipartisan criticism and Vance's declaration that he would not watch the proceedings. Trump's announcement leaves the firing-squad execution scheduled to proceed without a public livestream.

sources.news_title: BREAKING: Trump SCRAPS Pentagon's Firing Squad Livestream Plan for Fort Hood Jihadist Nidal Hasan
sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday that the scheduled firing squad execution of Fort Hood mass murderer Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed, reversing a plan the Pentagon had announced earlier this month.
In a post on Truth Social, the president confirmed that Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others at the Texas military base in 2009, "will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."
Trump wrote that streaming the execution "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," but added that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device."
The president said the execution "may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose," according to his post and reporting from Fox News and the Associated Press.
A Pentagon Plan Reversed
The Pentagon announced on October 5 that Trump had approved Hasan's execution by firing squad at Fort Hood, with the date set for December 3, 2026. Pentagon officials subsequently told the Associated Press that the execution would be livestreamed, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended the decision during an appearance on Real America's Voice on October 8.
"He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Hegseth said. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
The announcement drew sharp criticism from human rights organizations, the United Nations, and some officials within the administration itself. ABC News reported Tuesday that some officials had "raised concerns about the optics of broadcasting an execution," particularly one in which a firing squad would shoot a paralyzed man confined to a wheelchair, and worried the footage could fuel anti-American propaganda among Islamic extremist groups.
Vice President JD Vance and House Speaker Mike Johnson both said they would not watch the execution, according to ABC News."
The Crimes of Nidal Hasan
On November 5, 2009, Hasan opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center in Texas, killing 13 unarmed soldiers and civilians and injuring 32 others. Court records show Hasan told Army officials after his arrest that he had hoped to die during the attack and become a martyr, and said he would still consider himself a martyr if executed.
Hasan was convicted and sentenced to death. His execution would be the first military execution in more than 60 years and the first firing squad execution of a service member since World War II, according to the Associated Press.
Trump has consistently said the sentence should be carried out regardless of the livestream decision. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes," he said last week. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
The White House has not released additional details about what in-person viewing arrangements will be made for the victims' families. It is not yet known whether the Pentagon will provide any official recording of the execution for archival purposes.
The decision comes as the administration continues to weigh the balance between transparency and the potential consequences of broadcasting state executions. According to Amnesty International, more than 2,700 executions took place across 17 countries last year, but only two nations — Iran and Afghanistan — carried them out publicly.
Our Take
Let's be clear about what matters here: Nidal Hasan murdered 13 American soldiers in cold blood and wounded 32 more. He admitted he wanted to be a martyr. He is finally going to face justice after nearly two decades of appeals, delays, and bureaucratic foot-dragging. That is the headline that should never get lost.
The livestream debate was always a distraction from that core truth. Hegseth was right that the world needs to understand there are serious consequences for terrorism against Americans. But Trump was also right to recognize that many decent people — including gold star families who have suffered enough — simply do not want to watch a man be shot to death on their screens, even a man who deserves it.The president made a judgment call. He weighed the deterrent value against the human cost, and he sided with the victims' families and the sensibilities of everyday Americans. That is leadership. He did not cave to the UN's "abhorrent" pearl-clutching or the predictable cries from the international left. He made the call himself, and he owns it.
What the detractors fail to understand is that this was never about putting on a show. It was about making sure that jihadists know that if you attack America, you will pay the ultimate price. That message still goes out loud and clear on December 3.
The only question now: After 17 years of waiting, will the families of the Fort Hood 13 finally receive the closure they have been denied for so long?

sources.text:
US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former US Army major convicted of carrying out the 2009 Fort Hood terrorist attack, will not be livestreamed as previously planned.
In a statement, Trump confirmed that Hasan, who murdered 13 people and wounded 32 others, will still be executed by firing squad on December 3, but that the broadcast has been canceled following objections to making the execution publicly viewable.
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan, but many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device," Trump wrote.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the President declared.
Trump added that immediate family members of Hasan's victims would be allowed to witness the execution in person if they wished.
"They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he stated.
In his announcement, Trump also addressed Hasan's communications with radical Yemeni-American cleric Anwar al-Awlaki before the massacre. He noted that the FBI had intercepted electronic exchanges between the two but that investigators reviewing the correspondence had concluded that Hasan did not pose a threat.
Trump characterized the assessment, which he attributed to the Obama administration, as a major intelligence failure.
The reversal comes after 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other senior military officers publicly urged the administration to abandon the planned livestream.
In an open letter, the former officers warned that broadcasting the execution could damage the reputation of the US military, endanger American personnel, and provide extremist groups with propaganda material.
They also expressed concern that the public broadcast could allow Hasan to be portrayed as a martyr by his supporters.
"We appeal to the president, our representatives in Congress, and all citizens to act to prevent this clear and barbaric abuse of their authority," the officers wrote.
The Pentagon had previously announced that the execution would be broadcast live, following comments by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth confirming that the public would be able to watch.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said in an interview with Real America's Voice News.
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, carried out the terrorist attack at Fort Hood, Texas, on November 5, 2009. He opened fire on unarmed soldiers at a military processing facility after shouting "Allahu Akbar."
During his trial, Hasan acknowledged responsibility for the shooting and said he had acted to prevent American soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan and killing Muslims.
A military court convicted Hasan in 2013 and sentenced him to death. His sentence was subsequently upheld through the appeals process, and the Supreme Court declined to review his case.
Trump approved Hasan's execution earlier this month following a recommendation from Hegseth. If carried out as scheduled, it will be the first US military execution since 1961.

MAGA divides as the administration debates broadcasting Hasan's death penalty.
The United States is about to make history as it prepares to televise the first-ever execution by firing squad. Former U.S. Army Major Nidal Hasan will be put to death this December for a heinous crime committed in 2009. But while the original plan was to show the event to the world, the Trump administration is locked in a debate that could take the execution off air before it even happens.
A formal execution has never been aired on TV in the United States. The most recent public execution happened in 1936 in Kentucky after Rainey Bethea raped and killed a 70-year-old woman. He was hanged for his crimes, and since the first public broadcast network didn’t arrive until several years later, the only way to witness the event was in person. Needless to say, we’re in uncharted waters.
The broadcast could be used against the United States.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth gave the green light for the public execution, telling Jack Posobiec in an interview, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
These “things” Hegseth refers to are the 13 U.S. Army members that Hasan murdered on November 5, 2009. Hasan was later charged and convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. He was ultimately sentenced to death days later.
The execution will take place right back at the scene of the crime. On December 3, 2026, at 1 p.m. Central Time, Nidal Hasan will die at the hands of a firing squad. While lethal injection is usually the first option to carry out a humane death sentence, firing squads are still common in the U.S., with the latest execution taking place as recently as 2025.
The public execution of Nidal Hasan was meant to air on television and be available on streaming platforms in December. However, a new report reveals that the Trump administration is still debating the morality of putting a man to death in front of the entire world.
Vice President JD Vance has said he won't watch a livestreamed event, while Trump is reportedly cool to the streaming idea; according to ABC News, some within the administration fear that the broadcast could be used against the United States as anti-American propaganda or fuel for Islamic extremists, or that it could simply reflect poorly on the nation. The situation looks even worse considering Hasan was paralyzed during the murders in 2009, leaving him confined to a wheelchair. Visually, killing a disabled man on TV would not play well.
Despite internal discussions, the Pentagon insists that the execution will be carried out on air as planned. A list of supported TV channels and streaming services has not been finalized yet. However, some services have already pre-emptively barred the content from their platforms, including TikTok and Newsmax. Specific viewing details should be available as we get closer to the execution.

Sara Gonzales Unfiltered
In terms of the legality of the event, the FCC has strict laws that govern the content available on TV. Specifically, stations can’t display indecent or obscene material, nor can they propagate hoaxes or distort the news. One thing dubiously absent from regulatory scrutiny is violence. Violent content is protected on TV under free speech laws. That means a public execution is technically within the FCC’s rules.
Furthermore, FCC Commissioner Brendan Carr has made no threats to get in the way. In fact, he left the final decision to air the execution to Hegseth. So as long as the Trump administration sorts out its internal disagreement, the event will be available for all to watch.
The only question now is: Should you watch it?
Legally, the death penalty is a just process sanctioned by 27 U.S. states and the federal government. At least some of biblical Scripture supports the death penalty as well. Genesis 9:6 states, “Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed; for in the image of God has God made mankind." Spiritually — as in for the sake of your soul — it may be best not to tune in.
Just because the death penalty is legal and righteous doesn’t mean that it’s meant for the entire world to see. Watching someone’s life be taken siphons away a bit of one’s own soul in kind, and the spiritual trade-off isn’t worth the cost.
Without any more details, there is no way to know exactly how brutal the event will appear on TV. That said, the forceful end of a life is still a vicious death. Children definitely shouldn’t watch the event, and if you wish to protect your soul, you shouldn’t watch it either.

House Speaker Mike Johnson also said he would not watch the execution. In an interview with CBS News earlier this month, he said he had colleagues "who have concerns,” over the livestream, one of them being “that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists."
In addition to many Democrats in Congress, several Republican lawmakers also expressed their disapproval over the plans..

Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, an outspoken GOP critic against Hegseth, called the livestream “beyond disgusting. Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”

Hasan, a former U.S. Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 in a mass shooting at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

(LifeSiteNews) — President Donald Trump announced Thursday morning that he has reversed the decision to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan for his 2009 shooting spree that killed more than a dozen people at a U.S. Army base in Fort Hood, Texas, following backlash over the plan even from supporters of capital punishment.
Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who reached the rank of Major, came to oppose U.S. military action in Afghanistan and Iraq, and grew more radical upon learning he was slated for deployment sometime in 2009. On May 9 of that year, he entered Fort Hood with two handguns and went on a shooting spree, killing 13 and wounding at least 31, until he was stopped by a police bullet that left him paralyzed.
He reportedly shouted “Allahu Akbar” during the rampage, and it later came out he was a practitioner of Sharia law, had attended a Virginia mosque led by pro-terrorism imam Anwar al-Awlaki, and had previously advocated Muslims “ris(ing) up against the U.S. military.”
Hasan was convicted in August 2013, and sentenced to death less than a week later. Last week, the Army set his execution date for December 3 at Fort Hood, following approval by President Donald Trump. It will be the Army’s first firing squad execution since World War II. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the execution, sparking controversy and reports of dissent within and outside the administration.
Trump confirmed the reversal in a Thursday morning Truth Social post. After recapping some background on the case, he said:
I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!
Some defenders of the administration had championed the idea as a powerful deterrent statement, while others condemned it as a tasteless stunt. Catholic philosopher Edward Feser, known for defending the permissibility of capital punishment, had denounced the Trump administration for “bring(ing) discredit even to the otherwise defensible policies it tries to implement.” Archbishop for Military Services Timothy Broglio, in urging Catholic soldiers not to participate, asked, “Do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries” and “Does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?”
Public execution used to be commonplace in past centuries, with gallows erected in town squares for public hangings of criminals. But as execution methods became more sophisticated and societal mores changed, so too did the normalcy of displaying state-sanctioned killings. Today, members of the public and press may attend executions, but the last public execution in the United States was of convicted murderer Roscoe “Red” Jackson in 1937.
Capital punishment is one of the most contentious issues in modern politics, with ambivalence often crossing the usual partisan lines. Proponents argue it a necessary deterrent, that it is a key tool in pushing violent offenders to plead guilty in order to evade it, and that nothing less than death can adequately register societal condemnation for humanity’s worst crimes. Opponents argue death is irreversible in cases of wrongful convictions, that its implementation often constitutes “cruel and unusual punishment,” and that society should draw a hard line against taking any life when not strictly necessary to defend one’s self or others from danger (a standard liberal opponents do not apply to their support of abortion-on-demand).
In 2018, the late Pope Francis complicated the discourse about the religious permissibility of capital punishment when he issued a papal decree revising n. 2267 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church to declare that a “new understanding has emerged of the significance of penal sanctions imposed by the state,” and therefore “the death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person.” It also declared that the Church “works with determination for its abolition worldwide.”
The passage previously read that authorities should limit themselves to “non-lethal means (…) to defend and protect people’s safety from the aggressor” and “cases in which the execution of the offender is an absolute necessity ‘are very rare, if not practically nonexistent,’” but granted that “traditional teaching of the Church does not exclude recourse to the death penalty” when absolutely necessary.
Pope Leo XIV has doubled down on Francis’s direction, repeatedly describing the death penalty as “inadmissible.” Christian supporters of capital punishment point to Genesis 9:6 which states: “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed; for God made man in his own image.” Other popes throughout history, such as Pope Leo X, Pope Pius XII, and St. John Paul II, have affirmed the legitimacy of capital punishment in at least some circumstances.

sources.text:
The Pentagon said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and President Donald Trump are "completely aligned" after Trump rejected plans to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan, breaking from an earlier statement made by Hegseth.
Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told Newsweek, “President Trump and Secretary Hegseth spoke about the decision to not livestream Hasan's execution ahead of the Truth Social announcement. The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned.”
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that while Hasan was "a very bad and evil man" who would still die by firing squad, his death would not be streamed, despite the president feeling it "might have been a strong deterrent."
The president said, "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed."
"That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!"
Hasan shot and killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas.
The Fort Hood attack came at the height of the global War on Terrorism, and investigators concluded that Hasan was motivated by Islamic extremist beliefs. They cite his pre-attack email exchanges with Anwar al-Awlaki, the al-Qaeda-linked cleric who later praised the massacre, as well as Hasan's own statements. During his court-martial, Hasan said he had acted in defense of the Taliban, described himself as having "switched sides".
Hegseth said in an interview on October 8 that he planned to show Hasan's death publicly, marking the first such public execution in the U.S. for decades. Trump and Vice President JD Vance pushed back in the days that followed, and former military leaders also raised concerns.
Hegseth Plan Faced Bipartisan Backlash
Numerous Republicans have broken with the Trump administration on the now-scrapped plan to livestream the execution.
Vance expressed skepticism about the possibility and said he would not be watching.
"I don't know that that’s actually going to happen," the vice president told reporters last Friday. "So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people."
Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, wrote in a post on X that while he believes the death penalty is appropriate for Hasan, it is “beyond disgusting” to livestream it.
“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” he wrote.
Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, said on Friday that he would not televise or publicize the execution.
“If it were me, I wouldn’t televise it or publicize it or whatever they’re doing,” he said while campaigning in Michigan for GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers, NBC News reported. “I just think it makes—it makes our society coarser, and I wouldn’t do it. But there are arguments, you know, on both sides.”
MAGA Red Line Crossed, Poll Found
A new poll from ABC News, The Washington Post and Ipsos found broad opposition to livestreaming the execution. Only 18 percent of Americans support the idea, according to the poll. That number was 8 percent among Democrats and 14 percent among independents.
Even most Republicans said the livestream would be a step too far, with 34 percent saying it should be livestreamed and 64 percent saying it should not. A majority of MAGA Republicans (55 percent) said the execution should not be livestreamed, suggesting unease about the proposal among the voting bloc most loyal to the president.
Who Is Nidal Malik Hasan?
Hasan served as a military psychiatrist before carrying out the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, one of the deadliest attacks ever on a U.S. military installation.
Trump approved the execution by firing squad earlier in October. Hasan is expected to be executed on December 3, 2026.
Hasan was born and raised in Virginia to parents who emigrated from a town near Jerusalem to the United States. He joined the U.S. Army after high school and attended medical school through a military scholarship program. He worked at Walter Reed Army Medical Center, where he treated service members returning from combat in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Former colleagues and relatives said Hasan became troubled by the wars and the possibility of being deployed overseas.
On November 5, 2009, he entered a processing center at Fort Hood. Witnesses said he shouted "Allahu Akbar," Arabic for "God is great," before opening fire with a laser-sighted handgun. Thirteen people were killed, and more than 30 others were injured.
He was shot by civilian police. He survived but was left partially paralyzed. He has spent years incarcerated at the U.S. Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
Hasan has acknowledged being the shooter and described himself as a soldier who “switched sides.” He was convicted and sentenced to death in 2013.
How Do Firing Squad Executions Work?
The firing squad was last used in the United States in early 2025 in South Carolina after inmates chose it over other methods such as lethal injection or electrocution. It was the first time a firing squad was used in 15 years.
These executions typically involve a prisoner being bound to a chair with a hood over their head, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. A doctor finds the prisoner’s heart with a stethoscope and pins a target over it. Several shooters, one of whom is given a blank round, then fire at the prisoner, according to the organization.
When Was the Last Public Execution?
The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky is generally recognized as the last public execution in the United States. A report in a local newspaper, The Owensboro Inquirer, estimated that a crowd of up to 20,000 gathered to watch the 22-year-old man’s execution. Bethea, a Black man, was executed after reportedly confessing to the rape and murder of a 70-year-old white woman, but he was never charged with murder, Newsweek previously reported.

Julia Wilson was a civilian employee who processed paperwork for soldiers at the site where Hasan carried out his attack. She was nine months pregnant and heard gunshots from the parking lot as she returned from her lunch break.
She ran inside and hid in a computer server closet with coworkers, thinking, “They’re going to be cutting my son out of my corpse,” Wilson said.
Afterward, Wilson learned that as she ran to safety, Hasan fired 12 bullets toward her and her truck, but all missed.
As news broke last week about the livestream, Wilson said she grew upset hearing people treat it like a UFC fight or WWE wrestling event.
“People are saying, ‘I’m going to take off work. I’m going to tailgate. I’m going to have a barbecue,’” she said. “Hasan is 100% a monster, but he’s also a human being. He needs to pay for what he did. He knew full well what he did.”

“I think people, the general populace, really need to be aware of what happened at this event,” she said.
If people were offended by the decision, they could have opted not to watch, Platoni said.

At least 10 survivors of the 2009 shooting or members of their families have died by suicide in the 17 years since, Platoni said.

“The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” Parnell said.

Vance casts doubt on plans to livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter, says he won’t watch

Coakley saying the move was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”

The announcement earlier this month from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth that Hasan’s execution would be public – and subsequent confirmation from the Pentagon that it would be live-streamed – prompted significant blowback from both Republicans and Democrats, with many pointing out that the images could be used to fuel radicalisation.
Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell said Trump and Hegseth discussed the decision to drop the live-stream plans before the president’s announcement on social media.
“The secretary supports the president’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” Parnell said.
When asked how the public execution comported with his Christian faith earlier this month, Vance said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen.”
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said, adding: “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately live-streamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Vance is Catholic, and the church has long opposed capital punishment. Coakley saying the move was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.
Other top Republicans, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, voiced similar sentiments.

“Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump said on Friday when asked about the live-stream. As for Hasan and the method of execution, Trump said then: “He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad. I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on November 5, 2009, where soldiers were waiting in long lines to receive immunisations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted, “Allahu akbar” – Arabic for “God is great” – and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan could seek a lengthy delay of his execution, though given his behaviour at trial, he may not want to.

Reaction from Fort Hood shooting survivors
Alonzo Lunsford, a sergeant who had served in the Army since 1990, was among those injured in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting. Hasan shot him seven times -- including in the head and in the stomach.
Lunsford said that receiving the news that the Pentagon would not livestream Hasan's execution was "a sigh of relief," calling the administration's reversal a "very smart choice."
"We show that we’re a better nation and a better people than to livestream something like that," Lunsford told ABC News. "Even though what [Hasan] did and why he did it is messed up, it shows that we can rise to the occasion to be better than him or anyone like him."
Keara Torkelson was a 21-year-old Army specialist preparing to deploy to Iraq when Hasan shot her at Fort Hood. A shot to her back and a bullet grazing her skull led to medical complications and her ultimate retirement from the Army.
Torkelson said "removing the livestream is the right decision."
"Justice doesn’t need to be broadcast to be real, and the victims and survivors shouldn’t have to relive any part of this through a public spectacle," Torkelson told ABC News.
"For those of us who lived through Nov. 5, 2009, this is so much more than a headline or a political debate. It’s part of our lives and our story that we continue to carry. I believe there is a way to acknowledge accountability and justice while still honoring the lives lost, the survivors, and the families who have lived with the aftermath for nearly 17 years."
